title: HOSA Forensic Science: Forensic Entomology - Forensic Science - Forensic Entomology - PMI and ADH
subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: When forensic entomologists refer to Post-Mortem Interval (PMI), what are they most accurately calculating based solely on insect evidence?
options: The exact time the heart stopped beating
The time since the maximum temperature was reached
The Time of Colonization (minimum PMI)
The time since the onset of rigor mortis
questions.explain: Insects cannot determine the exact moment of death; they indicate the minimum PMI, or the Time of Colonization (TOC). This is the time elapsed since the very first insects deposited eggs on the remains.
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: What does the abbreviation ADH stand for in the context of forensic entomology?
options: Approximate Death Hour
Accumulated Degree Hours
Average Decay Heat
Atmospheric Daily Humidity
questions.explain: ADH stands for Accumulated Degree Hours, a measurement of thermal energy required for an insect to progress through its life cycle.
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: In ADH and ADD calculations, what is the 'Base Temperature' or 'Lower Developmental Threshold'?
options: The ambient temperature at the crime scene at the time of body discovery.
The highest temperature the maggot mass reached before the body was moved.
The temperature below which insect development pauses or effectively stops.
The average daily temperature minus the daily low.
questions.explain: The base temperature (lower threshold) is the critical temperature minimum for a specific insect species; below this, metabolic functions essential for development essentially halt.
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: Calculate the Accumulated Degree Hours (ADH). A species of blowfly requires 500 ADH to progress from egg to the second instar. If the constant ambient temperature is $20^{\circ}\text{C}$ and the base temperature is $10^{\circ}\text{C}$, how many hours will it take to reach the second instar?
options: 25 hours
50 hours
75 hours
100 hours
questions.explain: The effective temperature is $20^{\circ}\text{C} - 10^{\circ}\text{C} = 10^{\circ}\text{C}$. Using the formula $\text{ADH} = \text{Effective Temperature} \times \text{Time}$, we get $500 = 10 \times \text{Time}$. $\text{Time} = 500 / 10 = 50$ hours.
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: An investigator is calculating Accumulated Degree Days (ADD) with a threshold temperature of $10^{\circ}\text{C}$. Over three days, the average daily temperatures were $18^{\circ}\text{C}$, $20^{\circ}\text{C}$, and $12^{\circ}\text{C}$. What is the total ADD for this period?
options: 20 ADD
30 ADD
40 ADD
50 ADD
questions.explain: Daily ADD is calculated as $(T_{\text{avg}} - T_{\text{base}})$. Day 1: $18 - 10 = 8$. Day 2: $20 - 10 = 10$. Day 3: $12 - 10 = 2$. Total ADD $= 8 + 10 + 2 = 20$.
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: Which insects collected from the corpse provide the most crucial information for determining the minimum Post-Mortem Interval?
options: The smallest and youngest maggots found
The oldest and largest maggots of the primary colonizing species
The highest number of incidental insects
The adult flies currently mating near the body
questions.explain: To establish the time of first colonization (the minimum PMI), entomologists must determine the developmental age of the oldest maggots present on the remains.
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: When taking historical weather data to calculate ADH retrospectively, why might data from a local airport weather station need adjustments by a forensic entomologist?
options: Because airports strictly measure wind speed, not temperature.
Because the microclimate of the body (e.g., in a ditch, shaded forest) may differ significantly from the open conditions of the weather station.
Because weather stations only use Fahrenheit and ADH requires Celsius.
Because airports reset their barometric data weekly.
questions.explain: Microclimates dramatically affect insect development. A corpse in deep shade, a trench, or inside a vehicle will experience different localized temperatures compared to an open, standardized meteorological station.
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: In a laboratory, you are observing blowflies reared at $25^{\circ}\text{C}$ (base temp $10^{\circ}\text{C}$). If the pupal stage naturally requires 1500 ADH for this species, how many total days in the pupal stage should you expect?
options: 2.5 days
4.17 days
5.5 days
6.0 days
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: When a forensic team recovers a body and moves it to the morgue cooler, how does this affect the ADH calculation?
options: It resets the ADH counter back to zero.
It adds a constant 500 ADH to the total estimate.
It halts further significant ADH accumulation because the cooler is typically below the developmental base temperature.
It drastically speeds up ADH accumulation, as the maggots compensate for the cold.
questions.explain: A morgue cooler is normally kept at around $4^{\circ}\text{C}$, which is below the typical $10^{\circ}\text{C}$ threshold. This stops maggot development, so time in the cooler adds virtually zero ADH to the timeline.
questions.subject: Forensic Science

questions.q: How must the formula for Post-Mortem Interval (PMI) based on entomology be adjusted if the body is found indoors in a climate-controlled room ($72^{\circ}\text{F}$ constantly)?
options: Daily weather station fluctuations are ignored, and a constant ADH calculation based on the room temperature is used instead.
The PMI is automatically doubled because flies fly slower indoors.
No PMI calculation is possible since flies cannot enter buildings.
The base temperature must be subtracted from the outdoor temperature anyway.
questions.explain: Indoors in a climate-controlled environment, temperature fluctuations are practically negligible. The entomologist uses the constant room temperature to calculate thermal energy, bypassing outdoor meteorological data.
